idiom_name: HashMap<String, Value> / serde_json::Map with serde(flatten) for the open remainder
implementation_notes: Rust has no runtime member lookup, so the owner holds a map - HashMap<String, serde_json::Value> or the JSON-shaped Map<String, Value> - behind get/insert/remove/contains_key, and serde's #[serde(flatten)] on a map field captures the additional data that is not covered by the struct's other fields, which is exactly the fixed-plus-dynamic split. Where values are Rust types rather than JSON, dyn Any with TypeId and downcast_ref provides the runtime-typed slot, and deserialization of an unknown document into a map is the entry point for data-driven shapes. The classic structure is therefore hand-written, and it is justified only where the schema genuinely arrives as data (imported documents, metadata-driven models) rather than at compile time - convert to typed structs and enums once the shape is known, because the pattern deliberately gives up exhaustive matching.
pitfalls: #[serde(flatten)] is incompatible with #[serde(deny_unknown_fields)] - the docs state neither the outer nor the flattened struct may use it - so strict validation and an open bag cannot be combined on the same type.

Downcasting dyn Any requires 'static types and returns None on mismatch, and mutating through a shared reference needs interior mutability (RefCell/Mutex) whose violations (BorrowMutError, poisoning) appear at runtime instead of compile time.
Flattened maps make serde buffer content and lose precise unknown-field diagnostics, and a typo'd key is silently accepted as an extra property, so validation must be explicit.
HashMap iteration order is unstable, so any serialization or discovery that relies on ordering needs an ordered map (BTreeMap/IndexMap) instead.
